newsitem.title: UK: Iraqi crude still pricey despite cut - Euro lifter.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi crude still pricey despite cut - Euro lifter.

text.p: Prices for Iraq's Kirkuk crude will fall 10 cents a barrel in April in line with a Saudi price cut announced on Tuesday, but European refiners say Baghdad's oil remains too expensive.
"The reduction isn't good enough," a trader at a European major said.
"It's only 10 cents. And anyway it's not going to make a great deal of difference, because it has no effect on March barrels," another said.
They were speaking after Saudi Aramco informed lifters it would cut 10 cents a barrel from the value of its Arab Light grade for sale into Europe next month.
Kirkuk Blend, which is loaded onto tankers at the Turkish port of Ceyhan, is linked to Arab Light on a cent-for-cent basis under arrangements established by the U.N. oil-for-food plan.
The change puts the Official Selling Price (OSP) for Kirkuk at a $1.65 discount to international benchmark Dated Brent for April, compared to a discount of $1.55 for March.
This is the first change in price since the oil-for-food deal, under which Baghdad can sell limited volumes subject to strict U.N. supervision, was implemented last December.
But buyers are not celebrating, because they say Kirkuk for March loading remains uncomfortably pricey in a weak Mediterranean market awash with crude.
Traders say Kirkuk has traded on the Mediterranean spot market in the past two weeks at 10, 15 and 17 cents below the March OSP of Dated -$1.55.
"It's already difficult for the Iraqis to sell Kirkuk when you can get it on the spot market up to 20 cents cheaper," a senior marketing official at a European major said.

Traders said it remained an open question as to whether European lifters would make a fresh attempt to wring a more advantageous formula out of Iraq's State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO) for the second 90-day period starting on March 10.
"It's too early to know. People are going to want to be a bit careful. There is no point rushing to SOMO when we still have March barrels to sort out," said one trader.
The United Nations' plan allows Iraqi exports worth $2 billion over six months but permits no more than $1 billion in the first three months.
Term contracts run for three months, but traders believe Arab Light is too slow to respond to short-term changes in market fundamentals.
European refiners appear divided over prospects for widening the differential to Dated Brent.
Some fear there is little time to negotiate a change and get it approved by the United Nations before the first 90-day period expires next week.
Others say refiners have not made a serious effort to create a unified stance on the issue, the prerequisite for making an impression on the Iraqis.
"We tried to get prices down. We went to SOMO. But we are alone in this. We don't want to be the bad boys in this," a trader at a European major said.
"It has to be a combined effort because if one lifter goes to SOMO alone they will not listen," another trader said.
Traders are especially aggrieved because the United Nations sanctions committee last month approved deeper discounts for Iraqi crude sales to the United States.
"The U.N. moved the Basrah Light price, so in principle they could change the Kirkuk price. But in practice, it may be too late."

The price for U.S.-bound Basrah Light, loaded at Iraq's Mina al-Bakr Gulf terminal, dropped to $3.90 a barrel below benchmark West Texas Intermediate from March 10. The commiteee also allowed a special discount price of $4.30 below WTI for February and up to March 9, down from the originally agreed $3.85 under.
The committee also approved a request to change the structure of the price formula which determines the Iraqi crude discount.
--William Maclean, London newsroom +44 171 542 7646
